name: CO2 laser blepharoplasty

lead: CO2 laser blepharoplasty uses a carbon dioxide laser to cut and seal small vessels during eyelid surgery. It can be paired with laser resurfacing of wrinkled eyelid skin.
Small paired comparisons from the 1980s and 1990s report less bleeding, bruising and swelling on the laser side, with no long-term difference in cosmetic result.

paras: The laser vaporises tissue while coagulating small blood vessels, giving a drier surgical field than a scalpel [2].
General blepharoplasty risks apply. Published reports include a case of necrotising fasciitis after laser blepharoplasty and cases of strabismus after cosmetic blepharoplasty [6][10].

lead: CO2 laser blepharoplasty is eyelid surgery in which a carbon dioxide laser is used as the cutting and coagulating instrument in place of a cold steel scalpel and electrocautery [1][2]. It may be combined with laser resurfacing of the surrounding skin to treat periocular wrinkles [3].

Published reports from the 1980s and 1990s, mostly small series and paired side-by-side comparisons, describe less intraoperative bleeding and less early bruising and swelling with the laser, but report no long-term difference in cosmetic result or scarring compared with conventional technique [2][4][1]. Documented complications include a case report of necrotising fasciitis after laser blepharoplasty [5].

paras: The laser cuts tissue while cauterising small vessels, which is the basis of the claimed advantages: better control of bleeding and a clearer surgical field [2][1]. It can be used for upper and lower lid surgery, including transconjunctival lower-lid approaches, and for resurfacing periocular skin during the same operation [3][6]. A general encyclopedia account lists the cited benefits as less bleeding, shorter surgery, less bruising, swelling and pain, and notes some dispute about whether laser use counts as surgery [7].

A 1984 series of 40 patients with average 16-month follow-up described good control of bleeding and minimal postoperative bruising and swelling, with advantages and technical disadvantages discussed [2]. A 1987 paired comparison in 13 patients, laser on one side and cold steel with electrocautery on the other, found reduced operative time, bleeding, bruising and swelling on the laser side, but no difference in cosmetic end result or scars at long-term follow-up [4]. A 1992 comparison in 10 patients used the same split-face design [1]. A 1990 review weighed advantages and disadvantages of the technique [8]. A 1994 study of 36 patients examined ultrapulse CO2 resurfacing of periocular skin together with transconjunctival laser lower-lid surgery [3]. A 2000 report described laser blepharoplasty with orbicularis/septum tightening and skin resurfacing as safe and advantageous [6].

A 1998 case report described necrotising fasciitis from group A streptococcus after laser blepharoplasty [5], and a 2003 report described acquired strabismus following cosmetic blepharoplasty in general [9]. The 1997 ASAPS/ASPRS Laser Task Force survey summarised complications and practice patterns for laser resurfacing and laser blepharoplasty among surgeons [10].
CO2 laser blepharoplasty has been reported as a treatment for Morbihan disease, a chronic eyelid swelling condition [11].

Human studies consist of small case series and paired split-face comparisons: 40 patients [2], 13 patients [4], 10 patients [1] and 36 patients [3]. These report reduced bleeding, bruising and swelling with the laser but no long-term difference in cosmetic result versus scalpel surgery in the paired comparison [4]. No large randomised trials were found.
